title: Democrats see openings in the South after midterms | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

Following Democratic upsets across the South in the midterms, invigorated party donors and strategists are planning to target more seats in the region, starting with gubernatorial elections next year.

Democrats – powered in part by asurge in Black turnout– achieved broad gains this month, flipping Senate seats in Mississippi, North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas and coming within 2 points of doing so in Louisiana, a state President Donald Trump won by 22 points two years ago. The party also captured top offices in Texas, where Democrats broke a three-decade losing streak statewide, and Georgia, where Black Democratic women won the governor’s mansion and oversight of most statewide offices.

Those are signs, Democratic strategists say, of cracks in the GOP’s longstanding “red wall” in the South.

“The power of national politics has shifted from the Midwest and Northeast to the South,” said Georgia-based Democratic strategist Fredrick Hicks. “We are now an official battleground.”

At a recent gathering in Washington of the Democracy Alliance – an influential network of major Democratic donors – the group’s president, Pamela Shifman, pledged to continue funding year-round organizing in the South. The alliance’s spending this cycle included supporting organizations in Mississippi, such as the state’s chapter of the NAACP, which registered 17,000 new voters ahead of November’s election.

In one of the biggest upsets of the midterms, Democrat Scott Colom this monthtoppled Mississippi Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smithto become the first Black senator elected from the state since the Reconstruction era. Colomwon by roughly 8,000 votes.

Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves, is term limited ahead of next year’s election. Democrats say they are hopeful that Colom’s win – powered by a coalition that included Black Democrats, independents and some crossover Republicans – could provide a roadmap for their party’s eventual gubernatorial nominee.

“You’re not going to win just because you have an ‘R’ by your name,” Austin Barbour, a longtime Republican strategist in the state, told CNN. “The Democrat Party is going to spend feverishly in Mississippi next year. We’ve got to have the best candidates with the best message to run superb campaigns.”

Colom, who repeatedly argued for greater investments in the South during his campaign, stressed the value of supporting local organizers during an appearance at the private donor conference and received a standing ovation from attendees, according to organizers.

The midterm results show “we can win the South,” said Christale Spain, who chairs the Democratic Party in South Carolina. “The population is moving to the South, so we have to be invested in the South if Democrats want to continue to have power.”

Her state is slated to kick off Democrats’ presidential nominating calendar in 2028 and a flurry of events next year will draw the party’s heavy hitters to the Palmetto State, starting with a two-day summit in January that is expected to attract a bevy of presidential hopefuls.

American Bridge 21st Century, a Democratic super PAC that spent $2.2 million to help Colom this year, is planning to ramp up its spending in the South, including making investments in next year’s trio of gubernatorial races, according to its president, Pat Dennis.

Dennis said recent Republican moves – including Trump’s decision to elevate Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff – mean some of the president’s most unpopular policies still will loom over upcoming elections.

“They are going to continue to do what they feel like and that is going to continue to have major, negative downstream consequences for the American people,” he said. “And that creates a period of political opportunity for us.”

In an interview with CNN, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, the outgoing head of the Democratic Governors Association and a likely 2028 presidential candidate, exulted in his party’s gains in the South – though hefaced some criticismfor not having the DGA invest more in the successful campaign of Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa.

“For the longest time, we were left out, underfunded, sometimes even looked down upon,” Beshear said. “But over the last eight years, we have clawed our way back to the table.”

The new officeholders now need to deliver results if Democrats hope to build on those gains, he added.

“The American people gave Democrats an opportunity, not necessarily an endorsement,” he said. “Republicans were not bettering their lives. They were making them harder, and they gave Democrats a chance.”

(As for his own political future, Beshear said he will sit down with his family and advisers after his DGA duties wrap up in early December to weigh his options but an announcement on any White House plans “probably won’t be before Christmas.”)

Kentucky and two other states, Louisiana and Mississippi, will hold gubernatorial elections next year.

In Kentucky, two of Beshear’s close allies are running for the Democratic nomination: Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman and former state legislator Rocky Adkins, who has served as a senior adviser to the governor. Beshear said he’s “actively supporting” both in the primary.

GOP Rep. James Comer recently announced his candidacy for the Republican nomination and quickly drew endorsements from top Republicans, including Sen. Rand Paul and Sen.-elect Andy Barr.

Colom, a 43-year-old local prosecutor, campaigned relentlessly across Mississippi, edging out Hyde-Smith in places like DeSoto County in the Memphis suburbs that went for Trump by 24 points two years ago.

Priscilla Williams Till, a civil rights activist and cousin ofEmmett Tillwho lost to Colom in the Senate primary, has declared her candidacy for governor next year. Democrats are awaiting a decision by Brandon Presley, who lost to Reeves by fewer than 30,000 votes in 2023.

Among Republicans, state Auditor Shad White, Attorney General Lynn Fitch, Agriculture and Commerce Commissioner Andy Gipson and former House Speaker Philip Gunn all have declared their candidacies in the gubernatorial race.

In Louisiana, the field of Democratic contenders angling to take on Republican Gov. Jeff Landry still is shaping up. Landry is closely aligned with Trump, who last year named him special envoy to Greenland, amid the president’s calls for a US takeover of the semi-autonomous territory of Denmark.

Democrat Jamie Davis, who lost this month’s Senate race to Republican Julia Letlow by fewer than 26,000 votes, has signaled he is open to a run for governor next year or the Senate once again in 2028.

“You don’t get 720,000 votes and walk away with the metal hot. You keep striking the iron while it’s hot,” Davis told CNN at the What’s Next event for Democrats in Denver earlier this month, referring to his final vote tally.

He acknowledged that he’s a farmer, and is still learning much about politics, but that he’s spoken with both former Louisiana Rep. Cedric Richmond and current Rep. Troy Carter, and “they both applauded me and they both said they’d be with me on whatever I decide to do next.”

First, Davis said, he’s focused on the two House races going to run-offs, in Louisiana but “every day the phone still rings over and over and over again. People want to know what’s next, people want to know, ‘Hey, will you come to this event?’”

But Davis is still struggling to get known. Even in Denver, he was walking around with both a cap and a lapel pin with his name on it.

James Carville, the famed Democratic political consultant and Louisiana native, told CNN on Tuesday that looking back he regrets Davis’ loss, saying in terms of spending, “I would have definitely played in Louisiana.”

Businessman Gary Crockett, who lost the Democratic primary to Davis, announced his bid earlier this month. A slew of other Democrats have indicated interest in the race, ranging from Davante Lewis, a progressive activist who serves on the state’s Public Service Commission, to Gary Smith Jr., a former state senator who has touted a bipartisan record in the state legislature and whose wife, Katherine, is the great-granddaughter of late Louisiana Gov. Huey Long.

Toppling an incumbent like Landry is a heavy lift for Democrats, but “the ruby-red South just proved it can still flip,” said Lionel Rainey III, a national GOP political strategist based in Louisiana.

“No one is panicking,” he said of the Republican mood in the state. “The fire isn’t in the rafters, yet, but you can see it out the window.”

A spokesperson for the Republican Governors Association expressed confidence that GOP contenders can prevail at the state level with Democrats controlling both congressional chambers next year.

“Republican governor candidates have a better opportunity than ever to show at the local level that conservative, commonsense leadership is the best alternative to the radical ideas already coming out of Democrats in Washington,” Anna Marian Block, the RGA’s deputy communications director, said in a statement.

CNN’s Edward-Isaac Dovere contributed to this report.

CNN’s Edward-Isaac Dovere contributed to this report.
